## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4222429)Abstract

Venous thromboembolism (VTE), the third most frequent acute cardiovascular syndrome, may cause life-threatening complications and imposes a substantial socio-economic burden. During the past years, several landmark trials paved the way towards novel strategies in acute and long-term management of patients with acute pulmonary embolism (PE). Risk stratification is increasingly recognized as a cornerstone for an adequate diagnostic and therapeutic management of the highly heterogeneous population of patients with acute PE. Recently published European Guidelines emphasize the importance of clinical prediction rules in combination with imaging procedures (assessment of right ventricular function) and laboratory biomarkers (indicative of myocardial stress or injury) for identification of normotensive PE patients at intermediate risk for an adverse short-term outcome. In this patient group, systemic full-dose thrombolysis was associated with a significantly increased risk of intracranial bleeding, a complication which discourages its clinical application unless hemodynamic decompensation occurs. A large-scale clinical trial program evaluating new oral anticoagulants in the initial and long-term treatment of venous thromboembolism showed at least comparable efficacy and presumably increased safety of these drugs compared to the current standard treatment. Research is continuing on catheter-directed, ultrasound-assisted, local, low-dose thrombolysis in the management of intermediate-risk PE.

**Keywords:**Novel oral anticoagulants, pulmonary embolism, risk-adapted management, risk stratification, thrombolysis

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4222429)INTRODUCTION

Venous thromboembolism (VTE) is the third most frequent acute cardiovascular syndrome in industrialized countries, accounting for approximately 100 to 200 new cases per 100,000 population per year.[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4222429#b1-rmmj-5-4-e0040),[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4222429#b2-rmmj-5-4-e0040) As the incidence of VTE increases in an exponential manner with age, ongoing demographic changes will result in a growing number of patients suffering from the acute and long-term sequelae of VTE in the future.[3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4222429#b3-rmmj-5-4-e0040) Approximately one-third of all patients with VTE present with acute pulmonary embolism (PE), with or without clinically evident deep vein thrombosis; acute PE accounts for the majority of VTE-associated hospitalizations and deaths.[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4222429#b2-rmmj-5-4-e0040) The broad spectrum of clinical presentations of PE ranges from clinically silent thromboembolic events to sudden death due to fulminant right ventricular failure. The non-specific signs and symptoms of acute PE frequently hamper diagnosis, resulting in an underestimation of the actual frequency of disease. This is supported by data derived from epidemiologic models suggesting that only 7% of patients dying early in the course of acute PE are diagnosed correctly during life.[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4222429#b2-rmmj-5-4-e0040) In unselected patients, case fatality rates in the acute phase range from 5% to 15%, and it has been calculated that as many as 370,000 deaths may be related to PE in Europe each year.[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4222429#b2-rmmj-5-4-e0040)

This review elaborates on the risk-adapted diagnostic work-up and the acute-phase therapeutic management of patients with PE, highlighting recently published data and the revised guidelines and recommendations issued by the European Society of Cardiology (ESC) and endorsed by the European Respiratory Society (ERS). Particular focus is placed on the risk stratification of normotensive patients, the emerging role of new (non-vitamin K-dependent) oral anticoagulants for the treatment and secondary prophylaxis of acute PE, and the clinical benefits, risks, and indications of thrombolysis and other modes of reperfusion treatment.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4222429)INITIAL RISK STRATIFICATION

Rational use of diagnostic procedures to confirm (or exclude) the presence of acute PE, and subsequent treatment decisions, should be based upon a reliable assessment of the patient’s risk of early mortality or other major cardiovascular complications. The presence and severity of right ventricular (RV) dysfunction is known to be a crucial determinant of outcome in the acute phase of PE.[4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4222429#b4-rmmj-5-4-e0040),[5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4222429#b5-rmmj-5-4-e0040) Functional impairment of the right ventricle is due to thromboembolic obstruction of the pulmonary arterial vasculature causing an acute increase of RV afterload which results in RV dilatation, increased wall tension, and RV ischemia, which in turn perpetuate hemodynamic worsening. Overall, less than 5% of patients with acute PE present with hemodynamic compromise (shock or persistent arterial hypertension) on admission due to clinically overt RV failure.[6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4222429#b6-rmmj-5-4-e0040) This condition is associated with an estimated PE-related early mortality risk of at least 15%, a fact which mandates emergency advanced medical care.[7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4222429#b7-rmmj-5-4-e0040) Thus, initial triage of patients with suspected acute PE should be based upon the assessment of the hemodynamic (clinical) stability allowing for a simplified classification into a high-risk or a non-high-risk group. This approach allows all subsequent diagnostic and therapeutic strategies to be adapted to the acuteness and severity of the clinical situation, maximizing efficiency of resource utilization and potentially saving lives.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4222429)RISK-ADAPTED DIAGNOSTIC ALGORITHM

Based upon the initial stratification of patients into those with (suspected) high-risk PE either with or without shock or hypotension the ESC guidelines[8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4222429#b8-rmmj-5-4-e0040) recommend two distinct algorithms ([Figures 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4222429#f1-rmmj-5-4-e0040) and [2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4222429#f2-rmmj-5-4-e0040), respectively) for diagnostic work-up. Clearly, however, diagnostic approaches may vary among hospitals depending on local expertise and the availability of individual imaging modalities.

### Suspected High-Risk PE with Shock or Hypotension (Recommended Algorithm Shown in [Figure 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4222429#f1-rmmj-5-4-e0040))

Suspected high-risk PE is an emergency situation. Multidetector computed tomographic pulmonary angiography (CTPA) is recommended, if immediately available, for confirmation of the diagnosis. Alternatively, transthoracic echocardiography performed as a bedside examination for detection of RV dysfunction indirectly confirms acute “massive” PE.[9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4222429#b9-rmmj-5-4-e0040) Apart from verifying RV dysfunction (indicated by RV dilatation, paradoxical septal movement, abnormal motion of the RV free wall (McConnell sign), disturbed RV ejection pattern, triscuspid valve regurgitation, and dilatation and missing inspiratory collapse of the inferior vena cava) and pulmonary hypertension (increased tricuspid regurgitant jet velocity and/or pulmonary arterial dilatation),[8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4222429#b8-rmmj-5-4-e0040) transthoracic echocardiography may indicate the presence of mobile thrombi in the right-sided heart cavities.[10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4222429#b10-rmmj-5-4-e0040)–[12](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4222429#b12-rmmj-5-4-e0040) In unstable patients, signs of RV dysfunction on echocardiography are sufficient for prompt initiation of reperfusion therapy (e.g. systemic thrombolysis) without the necessity of further testing. Moreover, echocardiography may help to detect or exclude alternative causes of shock such as aortic dissection, pericardial tamponade, or severe left ventricular failure. In patients primarily admitted to the catheterization laboratory to diagnose or exclude an acute coronary syndrome, pulmonary angiography can be considered as an alternative diagnostic approach.[8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4222429#b8-rmmj-5-4-e0040)

### Suspected High-Risk PE Without Shock or Hypotension (Recommended Algorithm Shown in [Figure 2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4222429#f2-rmmj-5-4-e0040))

Pulmonary embolism may escape prompt diagnosis in hemodynamically stable patients, since clinical signs and symptoms such as dyspnea, chest pain, (pre-) syncope, or hemoptysis are frequently absent or, if present, non-specific.[13](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4222429#b13-rmmj-5-4-e0040)–[17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4222429#b17-rmmj-5-4-e0040) In this group of “stable” patients, diagnostic certainty is the physician’s first priority in order to prevent VTE recurrence but also to avoid unnecessary long-term anticoagulation which may, by itself, cause potentially life-threatening complications. The diagnostic strategy should begin with assessment of the clinical probability of PE using either validated explicit clinical prediction rules or implicit clinical judgment. In the past years, simplified versions of the revised Geneva prediction rule[18](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4222429#b18-rmmj-5-4-e0040) and the Wells score,[19](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4222429#b19-rmmj-5-4-e0040) both assessing the pre-test probability of acute PE, were developed and externally validated.[20](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4222429#b20-rmmj-5-4-e0040),[21](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4222429#b21-rmmj-5-4-e0040) Based on either the original or the simplified versions of these prediction rules,[20](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4222429#b20-rmmj-5-4-e0040),[22](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4222429#b22-rmmj-5-4-e0040)–[33](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4222429#b33-rmmj-5-4-e0040) D-dimer testing is indicated as a second diagnostic step before performing an imaging test in patients with low or intermediate clinical probability of PE (or PE-unlikely using a dichotomized score), whereas in cases with high clinical probability (or PE-likely), it is recommended to proceed to imaging procedures without laboratory testing.[8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4222429#b8-rmmj-5-4-e0040)

Plasma concentrations of D-dimers are elevated in acute thrombus formation due to simultaneous stimulation of the fibrinolytic cascade and formation of fibrin cleavage products. As the sensitivity and negative predictive value of ELISA-based D-dimer assays are high,[34](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4222429#b34-rmmj-5-4-e0040),[35](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4222429#b35-rmmj-5-4-e0040) PE can be safely ruled out in patients with low or intermediate clinical probability of the disease and a negative D-dimer test. These patients can be left untreated (i.e. without anticoagulation), as proven in outcome studies and a meta-analysis which indicated a 3-month thromboembolic risk below 1%.[36](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4222429#b36-rmmj-5-4-e0040)–[41](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4222429#b41-rmmj-5-4-e0040) Notably, in hospitalized patients, D-dimer measurement is of limited use. On the other hand, it is well known that the specificity of D-dimer testing (∼30%[42](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4222429#b42-rmmj-5-4-e0040)) is low and thus by no means confirms the disease but only indicates that further testing for PE is necessary. Several comorbidities or concomitant conditions, such as active malignancy,[43](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4222429#b43-rmmj-5-4-e0040),[44](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4222429#b44-rmmj-5-4-e0040) hospitalization due to other causes,[20](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4222429#b20-rmmj-5-4-e0040),[45](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4222429#b45-rmmj-5-4-e0040) postoperative state,[46](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4222429#b46-rmmj-5-4-e0040) pregnancy,[47](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4222429#b47-rmmj-5-4-e0040),[48](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4222429#b48-rmmj-5-4-e0040) or “simply” advanced age,[42](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4222429#b42-rmmj-5-4-e0040) can induce non-specific increases in D-dimer plasma levels. As recently shown, age-adjusted D-dimer cut-off levels (age × 10 µg/L for patients above 50 years) rather than the established fixed cut-off of 500 µg/L may help increase the specificity of D-dimer measurements;[49](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4222429#b49-rmmj-5-4-e0040) in a multicenter management study, the proportion of patients in whom acute PE could be excluded without further testing increased to approximately 30% without elevating the numbers of false-negative findings.[49](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4222429#b49-rmmj-5-4-e0040)

In all patients with a high clinical probability for acute PE, and in those with a positive D-dimer test, CTPA visualizing at least one clot at the segmental or more proximal level of the pulmonary arteries confirms PE with high sensitivity (83%) and specificity (96%);[50](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4222429#b50-rmmj-5-4-e0040) alternatively, CTPA may help establish an alternative diagnosis. Uncertainty persists with regard to the clinical significance of isolated subsegmental pulmonary emboli which were confirmed in 4.7% of patients imaged by single-detector CT and in 9.4% assessed with multi-detector CTPA.[51](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4222429#b51-rmmj-5-4-e0040) Poor interobserver agreement and the low positive predictive value of such findings justify further testing (e.g. with compression ultrasound) to confirm PE in this specific setting.[8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4222429#b8-rmmj-5-4-e0040)

Although CTPA has largely replaced other imaging modalities in the diagnosis of acute PE, a ventilation/perfusion lung scan remains a valuable, radiation- and contrast medium-sparing diagnostic option, especially for patients with contraindications to CT imaging (including those with severe renal insufficiency, hyperthyroidism, or contrast medium allergy) or in order to avoid unnecessary radiation in younger female patients as well as in pregnant or breast-feeding women. Compression ultrasound sonography visualizing proximal deep vein thrombosis also confirms PE without the need for further imaging tests.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4222429)FURTHER RISK STRATIFICATION OF NORMOTENSIVE PATIENTS WITH PE

Prognostic assessment of confirmed acute PE is based upon the patient’s individual risk of early mortality, taking into consideration the clinical severity of PE as well as the patient’s cardiopulmonary reserves and concomitant co-morbidities. As already mentioned, high-risk PE is characterized by overt hemodynamic compromise (cardiogenic shock or persistent arterial hypotension); this emergency situation demands immediate confirmation of the diagnosis and treatment to save the patient’s life. In hemodynamically stable (non-high-risk) patients with confirmed PE, advanced risk stratification intends to identify either patients at low risk for early (usually 30-day) mortality, who may be suitable for early discharge and home treatment, or patients at an intermediate risk who may benefit from advanced medical care, monitoring, and possibly early reperfusion therapy. Prognostic assessment should use a validated clinical prognostic score such as the Pulmonary Embolism Severity Index (PESI)[52](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4222429#b52-rmmj-5-4-e0040) or its simplified version (sPESI)[53](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4222429#b53-rmmj-5-4-e0040) ([Table 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4222429#t1-rmmj-5-4-e0040)). Patients with a sPESI score of ≥1 point(s) or a PESI class of III–IV represent approximately two-thirds of unselected PE patients and are characterized by a 30-day mortality rate of 11%–25%.[52](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4222429#b52-rmmj-5-4-e0040),[53](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4222429#b53-rmmj-5-4-e0040) These patients are considered to have _intermediate-risk_ PE.[8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4222429#b8-rmmj-5-4-e0040) In this subgroup, further risk assessment consisting of cardiac biomarker levels (such as, for myocardial injury, cardiac troponins I or T; or, for cardiac failure, natriuretic peptides), and the presence of RV dysfunction on CT or echocardiography should be considered. This enables patient classification into either _intermediate–low_ (RV dysfunction present _or_ cardiac biomarker levels elevated _or_ none of the two present) or _intermediate–high_ risk (presence of RV dysfunction _plus_ elevated cardiac biomarker levels), which will guide further treatment decisions.

In patients having a low risk of 30-day mortality according to the sPESI or the PESI, additional prognostic assessment using laboratory marker tests of or the evaluation of RV function by imaging modalities is not deemed necessary. However, if one or both of these tests have already been performed on admission, before (s)PESI calculation, and yielded abnormal findings (a sequence of events which is quite likely in clinical routine), then patients should probably also be classified into the _intermediate–low-risk_ category and treated as explained below.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4222429)ACUTE-PHASE MANAGEMENT OF THE PULMONARY EMBOLISM

### Anticoagulation

Anticoagulation prevents both early death and recurrent symptomatic or fatal VTE. The standard duration of anticoagulation should cover at least 3 months. Within this period, acute-phase treatment consists of parenteral anticoagulation (unfractionated heparin, low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH), or fondaparinux) administration over the first 5–10 days. Parenteral heparin administration should overlap with the initiation of a vitamin K antagonist (VKA), or it can be followed by one of the new oral anticoagulants dabigatran or edoxaban (see below). If rivaroxaban or apixaban is given instead (see below for studies), oral treatment with one of these agents should be started directly or after a 1–2-day administration of unfractionated heparin, LMWH, or fondaparinux. In this latter case, acute-phase treatment consists of an increased dose over the first 3 weeks (for rivaroxaban), or over the first 7 days (for apixaban).

The non-vitamin K-dependent new oral anticoagulants, i.e. the direct thrombin inhibitor dabigatran and the direct factor Xa inhibitors rivaroxaban, apixaban, and edoxaban, have been tested in large phase 3 clinical trials. In RE-COVER I and II, dabigatran was compared with warfarin for the treatment of VTE. The primary outcome was the 6-month incidence of recurrent symptomatic or fatal VTE. In the pooled analysis of the results of the “twin” studies RECOVER I and II, including a total of 5,109 patients,[54](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4222429#b54-rmmj-5-4-e0040) dabigatran was non-inferior to warfarin with regard to the primary efficacy endpoint (observed incidence 2.4% versus 2.2%; HR 1.09, 95% CI 0.76–1.57). Major bleeding appeared to occur with lower frequency in the dabigatran group, both during the period starting at first intake of study drug (which included the initial warfarin loading together with heparin treatment in the control arm as opposed to heparin alone until the switch to the oral anticoagulant in the dabigatran arm; HR 0.73 for dabigatran, 95% CI 0.48–1.11) and during the double-dummy phase (comparing monotherapy of dabigatran versus warfarin; HR 0.60, 95% CI 0.36–0.99).

In the EINSTEIN-DVT[55](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4222429#b55-rmmj-5-4-e0040) and EINSTEIN-PE[56](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4222429#b56-rmmj-5-4-e0040) trials, single oral drug treatment with the direct factor Xa inhibitor rivaroxaban was tested in patients with VTE using a randomized, open-label, non-inferiority design. In the pooled analysis of the results of both studies, including a total of 8,282 patients,[57](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4222429#b57-rmmj-5-4-e0040) rivaroxaban was non-inferior to standard therapy for the primary efficacy outcome (observed incidence 2.1% versus 2.3%; HR 0.89, 95% CI 0.66–1.19). Major bleeding occurred with lower frequency in the rivaroxaban group (HR 0.54, 95% CI 0.37–0.79).

The Apixaban for the Initial Management of Pulmonary Embolism and Deep-Vein Thrombosis as First-line Therapy (AMPLIFY) study compared single oral drug treatment with apixaban with standard therapy in 5,395 patients with acute VTE.[58](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4222429#b58-rmmj-5-4-e0040) Apixaban was non-inferior to conventional treatment for the primary efficacy, and major bleeding occurred less frequently under apixaban compared with standard therapy. A significant difference in favor of apixaban was also observed for the composite outcome of major or clinically relevant non-major bleeding (observed incidence 4.3% versus 9.7%; RR 0.44, 95% CI 0.36–0.55).

Finally, the Hokusai-VTE trial compared edoxaban with conventional therapy in 8,240 patients with VTE who had initially received heparin for at least 5 days.[59](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4222429#b59-rmmj-5-4-e0040) Patients received edoxaban at a dose of 60 mg once daily (reduced to 30 mg once daily in the case of creatinine clearance of 30–50 mL/min or a body weight <60 kg), or warfarin. In contrast to the fixed anticoagulation period(s) followed in previous trials, the study drug was administered for 3–12 months based on the investigators’ judgment; all patients were followed for 12 months. Edoxaban was non-inferior to warfarin with respect to the primary efficacy outcome of recurrent symptomatic VTE. Major bleeding or clinically relevant non-major bleeding was less frequently observed in the edoxaban group (HR 0.81, 95% CI 0.71–0.94).

Taken together, the results of the trials using new oral anticoagulants in the treatment of VTE indicate that these agents are at least as effective and probably safer (in terms of major bleeding) than the standard heparin/VKA regimen. Experience with the handling of these drugs in different clinical scenarios, and with the management of their bleeding complications, continues to accumulate, and useful practical recommendations have recently been published by the European Heart Rhythm Association.[60](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4222429#b60-rmmj-5-4-e0040) Currently, rivaroxaban, dabigatran, and apixaban are approved for treatment of VTE in Europe.

### Thrombolytic, Interventional, or Surgical Treatment

In unstable patients with high-risk PE, large-scale epidemiological data support the notion that inhospital mortality can be lowered by thrombolytic treatment.[6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4222429#b6-rmmj-5-4-e0040) Therefore, thrombolysis is recommended as first-line therapy in this patient group. Surgical and interventional treatments represent alternative options, particularly if the bleeding risk under thrombolysis is considered to be high and provided that the necessary infrastructure, equipment, and expertise are available on site.

In non-high-risk PE, the clinical benefits of thrombolysis have remained controversial for many years.[61](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4222429#b61-rmmj-5-4-e0040) Recently, a large multicenter, randomized trial compared, in a double-blind manner, thrombolysis with tenecteplase plus heparin versus placebo plus heparin in 1,006 patients with intermediate-risk PE.[62](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4222429#b62-rmmj-5-4-e0040) Patients had RV dysfunction confirmed by echocardiography or CT angiography, and myocardial injury confirmed by a positive troponin I or T test. The primary efficacy outcome, a composite of all-cause death or hemodynamic decompensation/collapse within 7 days of randomization, was significantly reduced with tenecteplase (2.6% versus 5.6% in the placebo group; OR 0.44, 95% CI 0.23–0.88). The clinical benefit was driven mainly by a significant reduction in the rate of hemodynamic collapse (1.6% versus 5.0%, _P_ = 0.002), while all-cause mortality was low, both in the tenecteplase and in the placebo group (1.2% versus 1.8%; _P_ = 0.43).[62](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4222429#b62-rmmj-5-4-e0040) On the other hand, the safety data were not favorable for thrombolysis, as the trial demonstrated a 2% risk of hemorrhagic stroke after thrombolytic treatment with tenecteplase; major non-intracranial bleeding events were also increased in the tenecteplase compared with the placebo group (6.3% versus 1.5%; _P_<0.001).[62](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4222429#b62-rmmj-5-4-e0040) These results indicate that routine primary thrombolysis is not recommended for normotensive patients with acute PE, unless they show clinical signs of hemodynamic decompensation.

An alternative to systemic full-dose thrombolysis may consist of local, catheter-delivered, ultrasound-assisted thrombolysis using small doses of a thrombolytic agent, provided of course that the necessary infrastructure, equipment, and expertise are all available on site. In a phase 2 clinical trial, 59 patients with acute main- or lower-lobe PE and echocardiographic right-to-left ventricular dimension ratio ≥1.0 were randomized to receive unfractionated heparin and an ultrasound-assisted thrombolytic regimen of 10–20 mg recombinant tissue plasminogen activator (rtPA) plus unfractionated heparin over 15 hours as opposed to unfractionated heparin alone. Reduced-dose local thrombolysis significantly reduced, compared to heparin alone, the subannular right-to-left ventricular dimension ratio from baseline to 24 hours without an increase in bleeding complications.[63](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4222429#b63-rmmj-5-4-e0040) The efficacy and safety of local, “pharmacomechanical” thrombolysis is also supported by the results of a recently presented prospective, single-arm multicenter trial which enrolled 150 patients with submassive or massive PE (Clinicaltrials.gov identifier: [NCT01513759](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/NCT01513759)).

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4222429)CONCLUSIONS

Venous thromboembolism has received relatively little attention from the scientific and medical community for decades. Recently, however, advances in diagnostic imaging, along with the development of new antithrombotic agents and strategies, increased awareness of the importance of VTE and began to improve patient outcomes in the acute phase and over the long term. The new evidence that accumulated in all these areas has led to clear-cut, clinical practice-relevant recommendations which are included in the recently updated ESC Guidelines on the management of acute pulmonary embolism ([Figure 3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4222429#f3-rmmj-5-4-e0040)).[8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4222429#b8-rmmj-5-4-e0040)

results.title: What's new in emergency medicine
results.content: In patients with intermediate-high-risk pulmonary embolism (PE; ie, biochemical and imaging evidence of right ventricle [RV] dysfunction), catheter-directed embolectomy is commonly performed but has not been compared with anticoagulation alone. In a recent randomized trial of 100 such patients, suction embolectomy followed by anticoagulation did not improve mortality but did result in a greater reduction of the right ventricular (RV)/left ventricular (LV) ratio (an indicator of RV strain) compared with anticoagulation alone (0.52 versus 0.24) . In addition, normalization of tachycardia and indicators of pulmonary artery obstruction improved in a larger proportion of patients undergoing embolectomy. The adverse event rate (including bleeding) was similar between the groups, as was the need [...] AHA/ACC guidelines for pulmonary embolism (March 2026) [...] Suction embolectomy versus anticoagulation in pulmonary embolism (January 2026)

ADULT RESUSCITATION

Catheter-directed thrombolysis versus anticoagulation in pulmonary embolism (March 2026)

In patients with intermediate-high-risk pulmonary embolism (PE; ie, biochemical and imaging evidence of right ventricle [RV] dysfunction), limited data suggest that catheter-directed thrombolysis improves RV function compared with anticoagulation alone, but does not improve mortality. In a recent randomized trial of 544 patients with intermediate-high-risk PE, ultrasound-facilitated, catheter-directed thrombolysis with [alteplase](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/alteplase-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link) reduced the composite outcome of PE-related death, cardiorespiratory decompensation, or symptomatic PE recurrence compared with anticoagulation alone (4 versus 10 percent); this difference was driven primarily by fewer episodes of decompensation (3.7 versus 10.3 percent) [[1](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/1)]. Major bleeding was numerically higher in the alteplase group (4 versus 2 percent) but was not statistically significant, and the difference in RV size at 48 hours between the two groups was also not significant. Interpretation is limited by low event rates, lack of blinding, and underrepresentation of patients >75 years. However, these data support our practice of performing catheter-directed therapies in patients with intermediate-high-risk PE. (See ["Acute pulmonary embolism in adults: Reperfusion therapy in intermediate- and high-risk patients", section on 'Catheter-directed thrombolysis'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/acute-pulmonary-embolism-in-adults-reperfusion-therapy-in-intermediate-and-high-risk-patients?sectionName=Catheter-directed+thrombolysis&topicRef=8365&anchor=H4140125415&source=see_link#H4140125415).)

Updated international Surviving Sepsis Campaign guidelines (March 2026)

The Surviving Sepsis Campaign guidelines have recently been updated [[2](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/2)]. The guidelines suggested that, while a mean arterial pressure of 65 mmHg should be targeted, a range of 60 to 70 mmHg is practical for most adults with sepsis. The guidelines also emphasized the importance of screening tools for early detection and management of sepsis, while discouraging both overly aggressive fluid resuscitation and empiric treatment for fungal and anaerobic bacterial infections, especially when suspicion is low. The guidelines encouraged active fluid removal (in the later phases of shock), rapid de-escalation of antimicrobials and, in mechanically ventilated patients, the use of selective digestive tract decontamination to prevent ventilator-associated pneumonia. We agree with these recommendations. (See ["Evaluation and management of suspected sepsis and septic shock in adults", section on 'Introduction'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/evaluation-and-management-of-suspected-sepsis-and-septic-shock-in-adults?sectionName=INTRODUCTION&topicRef=8365&anchor=H1&source=see_link#H1).)

Joint European and United States definition of refractory septic shock (March 2026)

Although sepsis and septic shock have widely accepted definitions, there has not been consensus regarding the definition of "refractory" septic shock. The Society of Critical Care Medicine and European Society of Intensive Care Medicine have recently proposed criteria defining refractory septic shock by the presence of (1) persistently elevated lactate concentration (>2 mmol/L [>18 mg/dL]) and/or prolonged capillary refill time, (2) lack of response to fluid resuscitation, (3) a norepinephrine base equivalent dose >0.5 micrograms per kilogram per minute, and (4) in those with suspected mixed shock, critical care ultrasound should be used to confirm lack of response to fluids and to exclude other etiologies for shock [[3](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/3)]. The impact of this definition on patient outcomes, such as survival, remains undetermined. (See ["Sepsis syndromes in adults: Epidemiology, definitions, clinical presentation, diagnosis, and prognosis", section on 'Septic shock'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/sepsis-syndromes-in-adults-epidemiology-definitions-clinical-presentation-diagnosis-and-prognosis?sectionName=Septic+shock&topicRef=8365&anchor=H8&source=see_link#H8).)

High-flow oxygen does not affect mortality in hypoxemic respiratory failure (March 2026)

Although frequently used, the value of high-flow oxygen delivered via nasal cannulae (HFNC) in patients with acute hypoxemic respiratory failure remains unclear. In a randomized trial of 1110 such patients, HFNC did not reduce 28-day mortality compared with low-flow oxygen [[4](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/4)]. HFNC led to a non-significant reduction in the intubation rate at 28 days (42.4 versus 48.4 percent), and rapidly improved patients' respiratory rates, dyspnea, and carbon dioxide levels. These data support our practice of administering HFNC only to patients with advanced oxygen needs (eg, >6 L/minute) rather than routine administration. (See ["Evaluation and management of the nonventilated, hospitalized adult patient with acute hypoxemia", section on 'Humidified, high-flow oxygen delivered via nasal cannulae (HFNC)'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/evaluation-and-management-of-the-nonventilated-hospitalized-adult-patient-with-acute-hypoxemia?sectionName=Humidified%2C+high-flow+oxygen+delivered+via+nasal+cannulae+%28HFNC%29&topicRef=8365&anchor=H3611214250&source=see_link#H3611214250).)

Updated resuscitation guidelines for adults (January 2026)

The American Heart Association and European Resuscitation Council have published updated guidelines for adult cardiopulmonary resuscitation and emergency care [[5,6](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/5,6)]. Resuscitation updates include: urgent electrical cardioversion for patients who are unstable and those with rate-related ischemia caused by atrial fibrillation or flutter; immediate defibrillation for all adult patients with sustained polymorphic ventricular tachycardia; and increased support for using extracorporeal devices for potentially reversible causes of cardiac arrest where resources are available. Post-resuscitation updates include a normocapnic ventilation target and recommendations for a target temperature ≤37.5°C for a minimum of 36 hours following return of spontaneous circulation. (See ["Advanced cardiac life support (ACLS) in adults", section on 'Management of specific arrhythmias'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/advanced-cardiac-life-support-acls-in-adults?sectionName=MANAGEMENT+OF+SPECIFIC+ARRHYTHMIAS&topicRef=8365&anchor=H7&source=see_link#H7) and ["Intensive care unit management of the intubated post-cardiac arrest adult patient", section on 'Setting the target temperature'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/intensive-care-unit-management-of-the-intubated-post-cardiac-arrest-adult-patient?sectionName=Setting+the+target+temperature&topicRef=8365&anchor=H1286775785&source=see_link#H1286775785).)

Induction and tracheal intubation in critically ill patients using etomidate or ketamine (December 2025)

Concern exists regarding induction with [etomidate](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/etomidate-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link) during rapid sequence intubation (RSI) in critically ill patients, particularly septic patients, because of transient adrenocortical suppression that may worsen outcomes. [Ketamine](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/ketamine-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link) has been proposed as an alternative for such patients, but it stimulates catecholamine release and may increase risk of myocardial ischemia or pulmonary hypertension. A pragmatic trial of more than 2300 critically ill adults undergoing RSI in the emergency department or intensive care unit found similar in-hospital 28-day mortality between the ketamine and etomidate groups (28 versus 29 percent) [[7](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/7)]. Almost half of the patients had sepsis or septic shock, also with no difference in mortality (39 versus 38 percent). These findings suggest that either etomidate or ketamine is a reasonable induction agent in critically ill patients, including those with sepsis. (See ["General anesthesia: Intravenous induction agents", section on 'Disadvantages and adverse effects'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/general-anesthesia-intravenous-induction-agents?sectionName=Disadvantages+and+adverse+effects&topicRef=8365&anchor=H262499028&source=see_link#H262499028).)

Updated sequential organ failure assessment score (SOFA-2) (December 2025)

An updated Sepsis Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score, termed SOFA-2, has been published [[8](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/8)]. SOFA-2 resolves many of the deficiencies of SOFA-1 (eg, inclusion of a broader range of organ failure thresholds in the original six organ domains). Data from over 2 million patients in over 1300 intensive care units (ICUs) were used to develop and validate the score in all-comer ICU patients. SOFA-2 and SOFA-1 demonstrated a similar ability to predict ICU mortality. A 1-point increase in SOFA-2 increased the odds of ICU mortality (odds ratio, 1.378). Sequential SOFA-2 calculations from ICU day 1 to 7 remained predictive throughout those seven days. We agree with the updated version of SOFA; however, it does not automatically change the SOFA-1-based Sepsis-3 definition for sepsis and septic shock. (See ["Predictive scoring systems in the intensive care unit", section on 'Sequential (sepsis-related) Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA)'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/predictive-scoring-systems-in-the-intensive-care-unit?sectionName=Sequential+%28sepsis-related%29+Organ+Failure+Assessment+%28SOFA%29&topicRef=8365&anchor=H889841588&source=see_link#H889841588).)

Arterial catheter in shock (December 2025)

Whether an arterial catheter should be routinely inserted in patients with shock is unclear. A recent trial reported outcomes comparing arterial catheter placement with no catheter in over 1000 patients with shock, half of whom had sepsis [[9](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/9)]. Ninety-day mortality was similar between the two groups (34 versus 37 percent). Pain, hemorrhage, and hematoma were more common in the arterial catheter group. Limitations of the study include a lack of blinding, baseline group differences, and limited applicability to specific types of shock. Nonetheless, these results suggest that many patients can be managed without an arterial catheter, although our approach is to place an arterial catheter when a reasonable indication is present (eg, labile blood pressure, unreliable blood pressure readings). (See ["Evaluation and management of suspected sepsis and septic shock in adults", section on 'Monitoring catheters'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/evaluation-and-management-of-suspected-sepsis-and-septic-shock-in-adults?sectionName=Monitoring+catheters&topicRef=8365&anchor=H3514478798&source=see_link#H3514478798).)

Capillary refill time as a tissue perfusion biomarker in septic shock (December 2025)

Preliminary data suggest that using capillary refill time (CRT) as a clinical biomarker of tissue perfusion may lower mortality in patients with septic shock. In a recent trial, a protocol that used CRT to tailor fluid, vasopressor, and inotrope therapy was compared with usual care in over 1500 patients with early septic shock [[10](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/10)]. The CRT protocol reduced the duration of vital organ support by 5 percent. The CRT group also received less fluid and had a higher percentage of patients receiving vasopressor therapy. However, mortality was similar, the trial was unblinded, and the impact of the additional components of the CRT protocol on outcomes was not accurately assessed. Nonetheless, these data support our practice of including CRT as part of the bedside assessment when monitoring the response to therapy in patients with septic shock. (See ["Evaluation and management of suspected sepsis and septic shock in adults", section on 'Clinical'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/evaluation-and-management-of-suspected-sepsis-and-septic-shock-in-adults?sectionName=Clinical&topicRef=8365&anchor=H1643153952&source=see_link#H1643153952).)

Tracheoarterial fistula: A large series description (December 2025)

Tracheoarterial fistula is a late, life-threatening complication of tracheostomy placement associated with high mortality. In a series date of almost 150 patients, the median time to fistula development was 80 days [[11](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/11)]. Only half of patients had the classic feature of an initial small "sentinel" bleed followed by massive hemorrhage a few hours or days later. Imaging (typically computed tomography) was better at diagnosing the fistula than bronchoscopy (80 versus 32 percent). Tracheostomy cuff overinflation and sternal notch pressure controlled the bleeding in over 70 percent of patients while waiting for definitive therapy (ie, endovascular or surgical repair). These data inform early recognition, diagnosis, and treatment of the most fatal complication of tracheostomy. (See ["Tracheostomy: Postoperative care, maintenance, and complications in adults", section on 'Tracheoarterial fistula'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/tracheostomy-postoperative-care-maintenance-and-complications-in-adults?sectionName=Tracheoarterial+fistula&topicRef=8365&anchor=H3292466807&source=see_link#H3292466807).)

ENVIRONMENTAL EMERGENCIES

Iloprost for amputation prevention in frostbite (May 2026)

[Iloprost](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/iloprost-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link) is a prostacyclin analog that is indicated for the treatment of grade 3 or 4 frostbite (ie, cyanosis that extends proximal to the distal phalanx after rewarming), but supporting evidence is limited. In a study with over 250 patients (80 receiving iloprost) in two Canadian regions that differed in routine iloprost use but with a standardized frostbite care pathway, iloprost was associated with a lower amputation rate for grade 3 frostbite (30 versus 53 percent) but not for grade 2 and 4 frostbite; patients receiving a higher total iloprost dose were less likely to have amputations [[12](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/12)]. In 40 patients with grade 4 frostbite, iloprost treatment was associated with fewer finger and toe segment amputations (40 versus 51 percent and 47 versus 58 percent, respectively). These findings support our recommendation for iloprost in patients with severe frostbite. (See ["Frostbite: Acute care and prevention", section on 'Iloprost within 72 hours'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/frostbite-acute-care-and-prevention?sectionName=Iloprost+within+72+hours&topicRef=8365&anchor=H1902794625&source=see_link#H1902794625).)

Microorganisms in children with freshwater drowning-associated pneumonia (February 2026)

Infection with gram-negative organisms, especially _Aeromonas_ species, is predominantly reported in patients with drowning-associated pneumonia (DAP). In a study from China of over 70 children with freshwater DAP in a pediatric intensive care unit, _Staphylococcus aureus_ was the most isolated organism [[13](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/13)]. Other common pathogens included _Mycoplasma pneumoniae_, _Streptococcus pneumoniae_, _Haemophilus influenzae_, _Klebsiella pneumoniae_, _Candida albicans_, and rhinovirus. These findings highlight the need for an empiric broad-spectrum antibiotic regimen, including coverage of gram-positive bacteria, in children with suspected DAP. (See ["Drowning (submersion injuries)", section on 'Pneumonia'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/drowning-submersion-injuries?sectionName=Pneumonia&topicRef=8365&anchor=H809358478&source=see_link#H809358478).)

Effectiveness of defibrillation in patients with hypothermia and nonperfusing shockable rhythm (February 2026)

Patients with hypothermia and nonperfusing shockable arrhythmias are less likely to have return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) with defibrillation at a core temperature <30°C (86°F). Current recommendations are to attempt defibrillation with up to three shocks but withhold further attempts pending rewarming since cold myocardium can potentially be injured. A registry-based study with almost 40 patients with cardiac arrest, a shockable rhythm, and core temperature <30°C found that ROSC was more likely if defibrillation was performed during rewarming, as compared with before rewarming (100 versus 25 percent) [[14](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/14)]. Defibrillation during extracorporeal life support (ECLS) had a fivefold increase in odds of ROSC. These findings support our recommendations to attempt defibrillation even with temperature <30°C and to not withhold defibrillation during ECLS rewarming at temperature >25°C (77°F). (See ["Accidental hypothermia in adults: Management", section on 'Ventricular arrhythmias or asystole'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/accidental-hypothermia-in-adults-management?sectionName=Ventricular+arrhythmias+or+asystole&topicRef=8365&anchor=H1808505299&source=see_link#H1808505299).)

Acute hypersensitivity reactions from rattlesnake antivenom in alpha-gal endemic region (February 2026)

CroFab and Anavip, antivenoms used to treat Crotalinae snakebite envenomation, can potentially cause severe allergic reactions. Anavip contains more of the carbohydrate moiety galactose-alpha-1,3-galactose (which is responsible for alpha-gal syndrome) compared with CroFab. A study with over 200 patients in Arkansas (a state with a high rate of alpha-gal sensitization) who received either Anavip or CroFab found that Anavip was associated with increased adverse drug reactions (including presumed anaphylaxis) compared with CroFab (22 versus 4 percent) [[15](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/15)]. Basophil activation testing from individuals with known alpha-gal syndrome found that Anavip more potently activated alpha-gal sensitized basophils. Clinicians who treat snakebite victims in regions with high rates of alpha-gal sensitization must be ready to manage anaphylaxis following antivenom (especially Anavip) administration. (See ["Bites by Crotalinae snakes (rattlesnakes, cottonmouths [water moccasins], or copperheads) in the United States: Management", section on 'Acute antivenom hypersensitivity reactions'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/bites-by-crotalinae-snakes-rattlesnakes-cottonmouths-water-moccasins-or-copperheads-in-the-united-states-management?sectionName=Acute+antivenom+hypersensitivity+reactions&topicRef=8365&anchor=H4098260420&source=see_link#H4098260420).)

GENERAL ADULT EMERGENCY MEDICINE

Fosphenytoin for trigeminal neuralgia attacks (May 2026)

Several pharmacologic options are available to treat acute trigeminal neuralgia (TN) pain, but available supporting evidence is limited. In a randomized trial that included 22 patients with acute TN symptoms, pain reduction on the numerical rating scale (0 for no pain up to 10 for worst pain) was greater at two hours among those assigned to [fosphenytoin](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/fosphenytoin-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link) than placebo (-6.1 versus -2.4) [[16](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/16)]. Treatment consisted of a loading dose followed by once daily maintenance treatment for up to four days. Patients assigned to fosphenytoin also had a higher rate of >50 percent pain reduction and reduction in the frequency of attack recurrence, and treatment was generally well tolerated. These data provide clinical trial evidence to support the role of fosphenytoin for acute TN exacerbations. (See ["Trigeminal neuralgia", section on 'Acute rescue therapy for patients with breakthrough pain'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/trigeminal-neuralgia?sectionName=Acute+rescue+therapy+for+patients+with+breakthrough+pain&topicRef=8365&anchor=H372586115&source=see_link#H372586115).)

AHA/ACC guidelines for pulmonary embolism (March 2026)

Several societies, including the American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology (AHA/ACC), have issued joint guidelines for the evaluation and management of pulmonary embolism (PE) [[17](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/17)]. The guidelines stratify patients by risk of PE-related death to facilitate management. Patients in category A (incidental PE), B (symptomatic PE with a low clinical severity score), and C (symptomatic PE with an elevated clinical severity score) require anticoagulation. Patients in category D (incipient cardiopulmonary failure) and E (cardiopulmonary failure) are candidates for reperfusion therapies (eg, thrombectomy or thrombolysis, if they have a low bleeding risk). We await adoption of this classification and encourage its use to facilitate management. (See ["Acute pulmonary embolism in adults: Treatment overview and prognosis", section on 'American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology/others'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/acute-pulmonary-embolism-in-adults-treatment-overview-and-prognosis?sectionName=American+Heart+Association%2FAmerican+College+of+Cardiology%2Fothers&topicRef=8365&anchor=H2148862999&source=see_link#H2148862999).)

Age-adjusted D-dimer cutoffs in deep vein thrombosis diagnosis (January 2026)

D-dimer values rise with age, decreasing specificity in older patients when a fixed cutoff is used to diagnose deep venous thrombosis (DVT). In a study of 2169 patients with low to moderate pretest probability for DVT, using an age-adjusted D-dimer (age [years] x 10 ng/mL for patients >50 years) compared with a fixed conventional cutoff of 500 ng/mL resulted in a 7 percent absolute increase in patients for whom DVT was excluded without lower extremity compression ultrasonography [[18](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/18)]. At three months, there were no VTE events in patients with a D-dimer level ≥500 ng/mL but below the age-adjusted cutoff. These data strengthen the case for more widespread utilization of age-adjusted D-dimer to diagnose DVT in older adults. (See ["Clinical presentation and diagnosis of the nonpregnant adult with suspected deep vein thrombosis of the lower extremity", section on 'Adjusted cutoffs'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/clinical-presentation-and-diagnosis-of-the-nonpregnant-adult-with-suspected-deep-vein-thrombosis-of-the-lower-extremity?sectionName=Adjusted+cutoffs&topicRef=8365&anchor=H410968138&source=see_link#H410968138).)

Andexanet alfa removed from the United States market (January 2026)

[Andexanet alfa](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/andexanet-alfa-inactivated-coagulation-factor-xa-recombinant-united-states-withdrawn-from-market-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link), a specific reversal agent for factor Xa inhibitors that was approved in 2018, has been removed from the United States market, as reported in a communication from the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) [[19](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/19)]. The communication mentions concerns about an increased rate of serious thrombotic complications compared with usual care in the ANNEXA-I trial and states that the company has voluntarily withdrawn the licensing application for commercial reasons. For life-threatening bleeding associated with factor Xa inhibitors, 4-factor unactivated prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC) can be used along with other hemostatic measures. (See ["Management of bleeding in patients receiving direct oral anticoagulants", section on 'Andexanet alfa'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/management-of-bleeding-in-patients-receiving-direct-oral-anticoagulants?sectionName=Andexanet+alfa&topicRef=8365&anchor=H635532401&source=see_link#H635532401) and ["Hemostatic treatments for anticoagulated patients with intracranial hemorrhage", section on 'Andexanet alfa if PCC is unavailable'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/hemostatic-treatments-for-anticoagulated-patients-with-intracranial-hemorrhage?sectionName=Andexanet+alfa+if+PCC+is+unavailable&topicRef=8365&anchor=H4272016095&source=see_link#H4272016095).)

Suction embolectomy versus anticoagulation in pulmonary embolism (January 2026)

In patients with intermediate-high-risk pulmonary embolism (PE; ie, biochemical and imaging evidence of right ventricle [RV] dysfunction), catheter-directed embolectomy is commonly performed but has not been compared with anticoagulation alone. In a recent randomized trial of 100 such patients, suction embolectomy followed by anticoagulation did not improve mortality but did result in a greater reduction of the right ventricular (RV)/left ventricular (LV) ratio (an indicator of RV strain) compared with anticoagulation alone (0.52 versus 0.24) [[20](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/20)]. In addition, normalization of tachycardia and indicators of pulmonary artery obstruction improved in a larger proportion of patients undergoing embolectomy. The adverse event rate (including bleeding) was similar between the groups, as was the need for intensive care unit admission and hospital length of stay; PE did not recur in either group. This study provides additional support for the use of catheter-directed embolectomy in patients with intermediate-high-risk PE with the goal of faster thrombus resolution and reduction in RV load. (See ["Acute pulmonary embolism in adults: Reperfusion therapy in intermediate- and high-risk patients", section on 'Suction/mechanical embolectomy'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/acute-pulmonary-embolism-in-adults-reperfusion-therapy-in-intermediate-and-high-risk-patients?sectionName=Suction%2Fmechanical+embolectomy&topicRef=8365&anchor=H3973928105&source=see_link#H3973928105).)

Post-thoracentesis ultrasonography for residual fluid evaluation (December 2025)

With the routine use of lung ultrasonography for therapeutic thoracentesis, it is unclear whether post-procedure chest radiography to still necessary to assess for residual fluid. In a recent prospective study of 147 patients with a free-flowing pleural effusion, there was excellent agreement between lung ultrasonography (performed immediately after the procedure) and chest radiography (performed four hours after thoracentesis; Gwet's agreement coefficient 0.93) [[21](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/21)]. There was also strong agreement between the proceduralist's interpretation and that of the blind ultrasound reviewer (kappa 0.81). These results suggest that ultrasonography is sufficient for evaluating residual fluid after thoracentesis; however, these findings may not be generalizable to patients with trapped lung and need additional study. (See ["Ultrasound-guided thoracentesis", section on 'Follow-up'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/ultrasound-guided-thoracentesis?sectionName=FOLLOW-UP&topicRef=8365&anchor=H9&source=see_link#H9).)

GENERAL PEDIATRIC EMERGENCY MEDICINE

Pediatric sepsis hospitalization and mortality in the United States (March 2026)

New estimates of United States sepsis hospitalizations and in-hospital mortality based on a pediatric sepsis event definition derived from the 2024 Phoenix sepsis criteria have been reported using electronic-health record surveillance of clinical data from over 3.9 million pediatric hospitalizations (neonates excluded) from 2016 to 2023. The average annual hospital incidence of sepsis was 1.3 percent (over 18,000 annual cases); overall in-hospital mortality was 10.1 percent (over 1800 annual deaths) [[22,23](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/22,23)]. Annualized national estimates remained stable over the study period. These findings update prior sepsis estimates based upon older definitions of pediatric sepsis and confirm the high burden of pediatric illness due to sepsis in the United States. (See ["Sepsis in children: Definitions, clinical manifestations, and diagnosis", section on 'Burden of disease'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/sepsis-in-children-definitions-clinical-manifestations-and-diagnosis?sectionName=Burden+of+disease&topicRef=8365&anchor=H632992306&source=see_link#H632992306).)

Ibuprofen for acute pediatric musculoskeletal injuries (January 2026)

Most experts recommend nonopioid medications as first-line therapy for acute pain in children. However, for children with acute musculoskeletal injuries (eg, fractures and sprains), some clinicians and caregivers have concerns that pain could be undertreated without opioids. A recent trial randomly assigned nearly 700 children with nonoperative musculoskeletal extremity injuries (primarily nondisplaced fractures and sprains) and moderate pain to [ibuprofen](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/ibuprofen-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link) alone, ibuprofen plus [acetaminophen](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/acetaminophen-paracetamol-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link), or ibuprofen plus an oral opioid ([hydromorphone](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/hydromorphone-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link)) [[24](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/24)]. Ibuprofen alone provided similar analgesia as the combined analgesia strategies and was associated with fewer adverse effects compared with ibuprofen plus hydromorphone. These findings confirm that nonopioid medications alone are sufficient for most children with acute musculoskeletal pain, and the addition of an opioid only increases the risk of adverse events. (See ["Pain in children: Approach to pain assessment and overview of management principles", section on 'Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/pain-in-children-approach-to-pain-assessment-and-overview-of-management-principles?sectionName=Nonsteroidal+anti-inflammatory+drugs&topicRef=8365&anchor=H15&source=see_link#H15).)

Lumbar puncture in low-risk febrile neonates (December 2025)

Current guidelines advise lumbar puncture (LP) to evaluate for meningitis in all febrile neonates seen in the outpatient setting, with an option to omit LP in selected patients 22 to 28 days old at low risk. In a new meta-analysis of four prospective cohort studies (1537 previously healthy febrile, full-term neonates <28 days old [meningitis prevalence 0.7 percent]), of the 632 patients identified as low risk for invasive bacterial infection by the Pediatric Emergency Care Applied Research Network (PECARN) rule, none had meningitis (negative predictive value 99.96 percent) [[25](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/25)]. These findings suggest that it may be reasonable to omit LP in selected febrile neonates after shared decision-making with parents/primary caregivers as long as they are managed by experienced physicians and other clinicians in facilities with adequate resources to closely and safely monitor neonates. However, LP is still necessary in the majority of febrile neonates ≥7 days old. (See ["The febrile neonate (28 days of age or younger): Outpatient evaluation", section on '7 to 21 days old'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/the-febrile-neonate-28-days-of-age-or-younger-outpatient-evaluation?sectionName=7+to+21+days+old&topicRef=8365&anchor=H857933794&source=see_link#H857933794).)

Botulism associated with contaminated or unlicensed products (December 2025)

Although botulism is uncommon in the United States, recent cases have highlighted the risk of contaminated or unlicensed products. Between August and November 2025, 37 cases of infant botulism were linked to a particular brand of powdered formula (ByHeart) [[26](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/26)]; the causative organism, _Clostridium botulinum,_ was detected in several formula samples and all products from this brand were recalled. In addition, three unrelated cases of iatrogenic botulism were reported following self-injection of unlicensed botulinum toxin products purchased from various online vendors in Asia [[27](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/27)]. Clinicians should consider the possibility of botulism and evaluate for potential exposures in infants with acute onset of weak suck, ptosis, hypotonia, and/or constipation and in older individuals with features of acute cranial neuropathy (eg, ptosis, diplopia, dysarthria, dysphagia) and limb weakness, particularly if fever is absent. (See ["Botulism", section on 'Forms of botulism and their sources'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/botulism?sectionName=FORMS+OF+BOTULISM+AND+THEIR+SOURCES&topicRef=8365&anchor=H6&source=see_link#H6) and ["Neuromuscular junction disorders in newborns and infants", section on 'Infant botulism'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/neuromuscular-junction-disorders-in-newborns-and-infants?sectionName=INFANT+BOTULISM&topicRef=8365&anchor=H14&source=see_link#H14).)

Rapid analgesia for sickle cell pain in the ED (November 2025)

Most individuals with sickle cell disease (SCD)-associated pain only present to the emergency department (ED) or day hospital when their pain has exceeded what they can manage at home. In a new study involving over 2500 children with SCD who presented to the ED with pain, receiving the first dose of an opioid within 60 minutes of arrival was much less likely to be associated with inpatient hospitalization, and receiving the second dose within 30 minutes after the first further reduced hospitalization risk [[28](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/28)]. Many children in this study received intranasal [fentanyl](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/fentanyl-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link), which correlated with faster time to first opioid dose. This study provides concrete evidence of how impactful rapid analgesia can be for individuals with SCD. (See ["Acute vaso-occlusive pain management in sickle cell disease (children and adults)", section on 'Give pain medication promptly (within 60 minutes)'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/acute-vaso-occlusive-pain-management-in-sickle-cell-disease-children-and-adults?sectionName=Give+pain+medication+promptly+%28within+60+minutes%29&topicRef=8365&anchor=H916987485&source=see_link#H916987485).)

PEDIATRIC RESUSCITATION

International guidelines for the management of pediatric sepsis and septic shock (May 2026)

The 2026 Surviving Sepsis Campaign International Pediatric Guidelines for the management of sepsis and septic shock in children are available [[29](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/29)]. The guidelines reaffirm the prime importance of the rapid recognition of septic shock and treatment that includes timely administration of fluid bolus therapy, empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics, and, in patients not responding to fluid bolus therapy, initiation of vasoactive medications (epinephrine or norepinephrine) ([algorithm 1](https://www.uptodate.com/content-not-available)). The 2026 guidelines also provide new recommendations that promote the use of blood lactate trends, lung and cardiac point-of-care ultrasound, and central venous oxygen saturation (ScvO 2 ≥ 70 percent) to monitor resuscitation. Our approach is consistent with these guidelines. (See ["Children with sepsis in resource-abundant settings: Rapid recognition and initial resuscitation (first hour)", section on 'Approach'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/children-with-sepsis-in-resource-abundant-settings-rapid-recognition-and-initial-resuscitation-first-hour?sectionName=Approach&topicRef=8365&anchor=H2493912177&source=see_link#H2493912177).)

Balanced crystalloid solution versus normal saline for children with septic shock (April 2026)

For children with septic shock, whether to administer balanced crystalloid solutions (BCS; for example, [lactated Ringer](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/lactated-ringer-solution-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link)'s) versus normal [saline](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/sodium-chloride-preparations-saline-and-oral-salt-tablets-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link) (NS) during initial fluid resuscitation is unclear. In a new randomized trial of over 8400 children with suspected septic shock, the combined outcomes of death, initiation of renal-replacement therapy, and persistent kidney dysfunction at 30 days were not significantly different in patients who were assigned to fluid resuscitation for up to 48 hours with BCS (3.4 percent) versus NS (3 percent) [[30](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/30)]. Hyperchloremia and hypernatremia were more common in patients receiving NS; increased blood lactate was more common in patients receiving BCS. Otherwise, adverse effects were similar in both groups. These findings suggest that either BCS or NS is an appropriate choice for fluid resuscitation of children with septic shock. However, the results may not be generalizable to patients with hospital-acquired sepsis or those treated in resource-limited settings. (See ["Children with sepsis in resource-abundant settings: Rapid recognition and initial resuscitation (first hour)", section on 'Fluid resuscitation'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/children-with-sepsis-in-resource-abundant-settings-rapid-recognition-and-initial-resuscitation-first-hour?sectionName=Fluid+resuscitation&topicRef=8365&anchor=H19450206&source=see_link#H19450206).)

2025 neonatal resuscitation guidelines (January 2026)

The American Heart Association/American Academy of Pediatrics/International Liaison Committee on Resuscitation/European Resuscitation Council (AHA/AAP/ILCOR/ERC) have published updated guidelines for neonatal resuscitation [[31-33](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/31-33)]. The guidelines reaffirm the previously published guidelines and neonatal resuscitative algorithm ([algorithm 2](https://www.uptodate.com/content-not-available)). Modifications include updated recommendations for oxygen concentrations during initial resuscitation of preterm neonates (21 to 30 percent if 32 to <35 weeks of gestation, ≥30 percent if <32 weeks of gestation to achieve target oxygen saturation goals); initial peak inflation pressures (20 to 25 cm H 2 O if <32 weeks of gestation, 25 to 30 cm H 2 O if ≥32 weeks of gestation); measurement of endotracheal tube (ETT) insertion depth from tip to upper gum instead of tip to lip; and smaller ETT sizes for premature/low birth weight neonates. (See ["Neonatal resuscitation in the delivery room", section on 'Overview of approach'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/neonatal-resuscitation-in-the-delivery-room?sectionName=Overview+of+approach&topicRef=8365&anchor=H2429918249&source=see_link#H2429918249).)

2025 pediatric advanced life support and basic life support guidelines (December 2025)

The American Heart Association (AHA) and the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) have published updated guidelines for Pediatric Advanced Life Support (PALS) and Basic Life Support (BLS). The PALS guidelines reaffirm the emergency management of children with [bradycardia](https://www.uptodate.com/external-redirect?target_url=https%3A%2F%2Fcpr.heart.org%2F-%2Fmedia%2FCPR-Files%2FCPR-Guidelines-Files%2F2025-Algorithms%2FAlgorithm-PALS-Bradycardia-250121.pdf%3Fsc_lang%3Den&token=q1pyrfBCbwFQJhc%2FMhbXjoDdj37GKNcvBArRruz4pi6prBWUwv9beMvsqP%2FK2xAfbvK884G79KE6fdnFMRXMM4fZAcZ5TzU5KFZrr6%2B23CknCjswgsstcbNI3gFKwwenEkwPM2igGHKUxJXjffIQ8On7WMAqa%2BQE8j%2BSsDFvZM4%3D&TOPIC_ID=8365), [tachycardia](https://www.uptodate.com/external-redirect?target_url=https%3A%2F%2Fcpr.heart.org%2F-%2Fmedia%2FCPR-Files%2FCPR-Guidelines-Files%2F2025-Algorithms%2FAlgorithm-PALS-Tachyarrhythmia-250117.pdf%3Fsc_lang%3Den&token=bMVDu3EwdQxRH00JMQHDLRQwGh1cclKlOyJ0Sl09whnFFbUzXKhrVbaEd0twQsKDKZjLqxYL5bwFayuhT%2FmkzZ0d%2FE6OdY%2F3%2BgP5rQmOblEgtT9hTOIra%2F%2Bln2i5svyPWGqh95oZeYA7moAvA%2FOIk%2BltqJ183iDuQJnlXkoVZgg%3D&TOPIC_ID=8365), and [pulseless arrest](https://www.uptodate.com/external-redirect?target_url=https%3A%2F%2Fcpr.heart.org%2F-%2Fmedia%2FCPR-Files%2FCPR-Guidelines-Files%2F2025-Algorithms%2FAlgorithm-PALS-CA-250123.pdf%3Fsc_lang%3Den&token=1lOXrl%2BAUwYFmmQHMw%2BxoR268snn0ENhenLHVT3D6c4bcZBFrNH%2F1HzPV2NrM9tbTMnz%2F0fSV%2B5hrAopPfQH6oKx9IyimzNo6fX%2BOAopVjZKTuKmCoo8d7Kpsf91LV9EHBS7jb49W6DIr7zXUYKCNA%3D%3D&TOPIC_ID=8365). During cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR), PALS advises end-tidal CO 2 monitoring when feasible and new diastolic blood pressure goals of 25 mmHg in infants and ≥30 mmHg in children when invasive arterial monitoring is available [[34](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/34)].
